[34mInvestigated:[0m Code paths in tinydb/storages.py (JSONStorage read/write and handle lifecycle) and tinydb/table.py (_read_table, _update_table, and every read and write call site). Ran scripts/bench_read.py on a generated 161,320-document, 40.9 MB database. Ran the test suite, which failed at first on pytest-cov addopts in pytest.ini and passed once addopts was cleared. Timed the cost of file read, encoding, and blake2b hashing on a 40 MB file.

[33mLearned:[0m Every Table read funnels through _read_table, and every write goes through _update_table, which does a full read before its write and clears the query cache afterward. Before the change, json.load took about 365 ms on the benchmark file, and blake2b hashing of 40 MB cost about 60 ms, which made it too expensive for a per-read check. Mtime and size are unreliable for freshness on NFS, so the check has to look at the file contents. Python's str hash is randomized per process, which is acceptable because the cache lives in one process.

[32mCompleted:[0m JSONStorage now keeps a parse cache keyed by (length, hash of text). read() still reads the file each call but skips json.loads when the text is unchanged. write() stores the data it just wrote as the cache. Table._update_table invalidates the cache when an updater raises, and JSONStorage gained invalidate_cache(). Added tests/test_storages.py with two tests covering external same-length rewrites and failed updates. The full suite passes with 230 tests. Benchmark: storage.read() dropped from about 365 ms to 44 ms, and uncached search from about 340 ms to 72 ms. Changes are uncommitted in tinydb/storages.py, tinydb/table.py, and tests/test_storages.py.

[35mNext Steps:[0m Waiting for the user to decide whether to commit the current changes or to take on the cost of wrapping every dict in a Document, which dominates db.all() at about 326 ms and is not affected by this change.

[36mNotes:[0m The cache returns shared nested objects, so callers that mutate returned data will affect later reads. The (length, hash) check is non-cryptographic and could in principle miss a same-length edit that collides, which is negligible for a trusted importer. Benchmark numbers come from one local run and have not been measured on the NFS share. The remaining ~44 ms per read is the cost of reading and hashing the file, and a generation token written by the importer would be needed to remove it.
